issues.legal_issue: A purchaser of part of mortgaged property is bound by a sale under the mortgagee’s power of sale without separate notice where the required notice was served on a mortgagor who retained an interest, and the purchaser knew of the power of sale and there was no fraud or collusion.
material_facts: The mortgage deed gave the mortgagee a power to sell without court intervention.
The purchaser bought only a small portion of the mortgaged property; the mortgagors retained an interest in the property.
The purchaser knew of the power of sale and included contractual protections in the purchase deed against the risk that the property would not be released from the mortgage.
Notice requiring payment was served on the mortgagors, but not on the purchaser, before the property was sold under the power of sale.
The courts found no fraud or collusion in the sale.
issues.conclusion: The sale was not invalid for want of separate notice to the purchaser and bound the purchaser’s interest.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 69(1) and 69(2) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, a mortgagee may exercise a contractual power of sale without court intervention in the specified circumstances, and the required notice may be served on the mortgagor or one of several mortgagors. A transferee who acquires only part of the property while the mortgagors retain an interest takes subject to the position created by notice to the mortgagors, particularly when the transferee knows of the power of sale and there is no fraud or collusion. Muncherji Furdoonji Mehta v. Noor Mahomedbhoy Jairaibhoy Pirbhoy was distinguished because it did not address section 69 and involved a mortgage deed expressly requiring notice to assigns; Hoole v. Smith was distinguished because its mortgage deed expressly named assigns as persons to be notified.

rule.if: challenge_to_mortgagee_power_sale and notice_served_on_mortgagor and payment_default_after_notice and mortgagor_retained_interest and purchaser_acquired_partial_interest and purchaser_knew_of_sale_power and not fraud_or_collusion

predicates.challenge_to_mortgagee_power_sale: The proceeding challenges a sale made under a mortgagee’s power to sell without court intervention.
predicates.notice_served_on_mortgagor: The mortgagee served the required payment notice on a mortgagor.
predicates.payment_default_after_notice: The mortgagor failed to pay after receiving the notice.
predicates.mortgagor_retained_interest: The mortgagor retained an interest in the property when the purchaser acquired part of it.
predicates.purchaser_acquired_partial_interest: The purchaser acquired less than the whole mortgaged property from the mortgagor.
predicates.purchaser_knew_of_sale_power: The purchaser knew that the mortgage included a power of sale.
predicates.fraud_or_collusion: Fraud or collusion occurred in connection with the sale.
predicates.sale_binds_purchaser_without_separate_no: The sale binds the purchaser even though the purchaser did not receive a separate notice.

issues.definition: When a challenge to a mortgagee’s power-of-sale transaction involves notice to a mortgagor who retained an interest, a purchaser of only part of the property who knew of the sale power is bound by the sale without separate notice if there was no fraud or collusion and payment default followed the notice.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser who knew that the property was mortgaged and whose purchase arrangements recognized the risk of its being sold to satisfy the mortgage cannot claim the value of improvements on the basis that the purchaser believed in good faith that they were absolutely entitled to the property.
material_facts: The purchaser bought a small portion of property that was already subject to a mortgage.
The purchaser knew of the mortgage and that the vendors could lose the property if they did not pay the mortgage money after notice.
The purchase deed required the vendors to obtain release of the property from the mortgage and allowed the purchaser to pursue that obligation and claim indemnity if they failed to do so.
The purchaser made improvements and sought their value after the property was sold under the mortgagee’s power of sale.
issues.conclusion: Section 51 of the Transfer of Property Act did not apply, and the purchaser was not entitled to the value of the improvements under that section.
issues.legal_principle: Section 51 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 applies where a transferee makes improvements in good faith believing that they are absolutely entitled to the property and is later evicted by a person with a better title. The purchaser’s knowledge of the mortgage, the limited nature of the purchase, and the contractual protection against the risk of sale meant that the purchaser could not have held the required belief. Narayana Rao v. Basava... was considered but held inapplicable to these facts.

predicates.claim_for_improvement_value: The proceeding includes a claim by a transferee for the value of improvements made to immovable property.
predicates.purchaser_knew_property_was_mortgaged: The purchaser knew that the property was subject to a mortgage.
predicates.purchaser_purchase_recognized_risk_of_mo: The purchase arrangements addressed the possibility that the property would not be released from the mortgage and could be sold to satisfy it.
predicates.purchaser_could_not_believe_absolute_ent: The purchaser’s knowledge and purchase arrangements meant that the purchaser could not believe in good faith that they were absolutely entitled to the property.
predicates.no_improvement_compensation_under_absolu: The purchaser is not entitled to improvement compensation under the rule for a transferee who believed in absolute entitlement.

issues.definition: A transferee who claims improvement value but knew of the mortgage and whose purchase recognized the risk of a mortgage sale receives no compensation under the absolute-entitlement rule when those circumstances preclude a good-faith belief in absolute entitlement.
